figures.caption: Figure 1: The shape of the invariant measure µ∞(dv, dx) of (V α t , Xα t ). Parameters: b(v) = 0, α = 1, τ = 0.5, U = 0.3, f(v) =max(0, v)2.

Figure 2: Raster plot of the finite neuron system associated to parameters (1.4). Each dot corresponds to a spike of a neuron. We observe a very strong periodic behavior at a frequency that is much lower than the neurons’ firing rates.

Figure 3: The Nyquist curve Θ̂α(iω), ω ∈ R, for the parameters (1.4) (α = 0.4). The winding number of the curve around the point (1, 0) is equal to 2: the equation Θ̂α(z) = 1 has therefore two solutions in the half-plane R(z) > 0. We deduce that the invariant distribution is unstable.

Figure 4: Simulation of the model (5.1) for β = 0.08, b(x) = 3/2 − x. We see that in the range α ∈ [0, 0.75], there is uniqueness of the invariant probability measure. Stability does not hold in an interval, suggesting Hopf bifurcations. We study the effect of the parameters U and τ on the stability of the invariant distribution. We see that increasing U or decreasing τ tends to increase the range of stability of the invariant distribution.
Figure 5: Number of invariant distributions of the 1D equivalent model and the 2D model.

Figure 6: Plot of Jeff = JEXt as a function of time. We observe that the dynamics explores the two critical parameters of the 1D model, which are J0 = 2 and J1 = 4.6. For Jeff ∈ (J0, J1), the dynamics of the 1D-model is bistable (two stable invariant distributions).
